title: GPU-Native Operators in Ray Data | Anyscale
gist: Ray Data added a GPU-native cuDF batch format and a RapidsMPF-based GPU shuffle backend built with NVIDIA, delivering up to 15.7x faster hashing and up to 4x faster end-to-end fuzzy-deduplication pipelines for foundation-model data curation, translating to roughly 3x better TCO than CPU clusters at small scale -- though GPU shuffle speedup diminishes sharply as node count grows for this workload.

themes.theme: What shipped: cuDF batch format and GPU shuffle

insights.claim: Ray Data's map_batches now accepts batch_format='cudf', handing user-defined functions a GPU-resident cudf.DataFrame instead of a pandas DataFrame or Arrow table, removing the need for users to manually convert data formats to get GPU-accelerated dataframe operations inside their Ray Data pipelines.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: Lowers the engineering effort for teams wanting to run cuDF-accelerated transforms inside existing Ray Data pipelines without hand-rolled format conversion.
insights.locator: cuDF as a first-class batch format

insights.claim: A new GPU-native shuffle backend built on RapidsMPF lets repartition and hash-aggregation operations run with ranks communicating directly over UCXX using RDMA or NVLink transports, skipping both the CPU and the Ray object store entirely for shuffled data.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: A structurally different shuffle path (bypassing the object store) than Ray Data's own CPU-based Shuffle V2 redesign -- signals two parallel shuffle architectures now coexist depending on whether GPUs are available.

insights.claim: On the compute-intensive MinHash signature generation stage of a fuzzy document deduplication pipeline (FineWeb 10BT dataset), cuDF-based GPU hashing is 15x to 15.7x faster than a NumPy-based CPU baseline across 2, 4, and 8-node clusters.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: A large, consistent speedup for a compute-bound stage of the standard data-curation pipeline used to prepare foundation-model pretraining corpora.

insights.claim: The shuffle-intensive grouping and connected-components stages show sharply diminishing GPU speedup as cluster size grows -- 3.0x at 2 nodes, 2.4x at 4 nodes, only 1.5x at 8 nodes -- because adding more GPUs added communication overhead for this dataset size, implying 2 GPUs was actually the optimal configuration and the dataset was too small to benefit from all 8.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: An honest limitation: GPU shuffle acceleration does not scale linearly with node count and can actually be cost-suboptimal to over-provision -- a caveat against blanket 'more GPUs always wins' claims for shuffle-heavy workloads.

insights.claim: End-to-end, the GPU-accelerated pipeline is 4.0x faster and delivers 3.1x better total cost of ownership than the cheapest CPU configuration at 2 nodes, narrowing to 2.7x faster and 2.2x better TCO by 8 nodes as the shuffle stages' diminishing returns dominate.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: Directly supports the article's headline '3x better TCO' claim while also showing that claim is strongest at small cluster sizes and weakens as clusters grow for this workload -- important nuance for cost modeling.

insights.claim: The GPU instances used in benchmarking (g6.4xlarge, $1.32/hour) cost only about 27% more per hour than the CPU instances used as baseline (m8id.4xlarge, $1.04/hour), yet deliver 3x-15x faster compute on key stages -- the small hourly cost premium is the basis for the reported TCO improvement.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: A concrete unit-economics data point relevant to anyone comparing GPU versus CPU instance choices for data-curation workloads specifically (not general compute).

insights.claim: Anyscale's next planned step is operator fusion between sequential cuDF and RapidsMPF operators to keep data resident in GPU memory and avoid unnecessary host-to-device round trips between pipeline stages, which the team frames as a 'significant step change' still ahead of the results already reported.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
insights.so_what: Signals the reported speedups (up to 15x on hashing, 3-4x end-to-end) are not yet the ceiling for this GPU-native architecture.

insights.claim: GPU shuffle support is planned to extend beyond deduplication workloads to Ray Data's preprocessor API, targeting feature-engineering pipelines as the next class of workloads to pick up the GPU path.
insights.speaker: Richard Liaw et al.
